text: Please note the new progress.  I have a new idea, that DLN (differentiable logic network) will perform AR and memory consolidation using distributive representations.  A symbolic logic engine can co-exist with DLN as the latter also respects logic structure.  However if the symbolic engine also performs AR or generalizations then it may seem redundant.  We are disucssing what exactly should be the role of the symbolic engine.
I am thinking if there could be some ways that a parallel symbolic engine might accelerate learning and convergence?  What do you think?

I am thinking of a hopefully more "decisive advantage".  An example:  human tells LLM, "don't forget to activate venv before running python programs".  This can be stored in the prompt as a directive.  In current LLMs, thoughts are either in the prompt (working memory) or in the weights (= inference rules).  In our architecture, thoughts can be: 1) in WM, 2) in DLN weights, or in the symbolic engine 3) as explicit facts or 4) rules.  If we (users) tell an LLM something, it immediately changes behavior because the directive is stored in WM (the prompt).  Ideally, we expect a thought to: 1) immediately participate in logic inference, 2) go into memory consolidation in the long term.  In an LLM, once the prompt is cleared, the thoughts are forgotten, so its ability to learn from live experience is limited. How might an AGI learn from experience better? A thought in WM does not enter soft memory consolidation, but if it is reflected into a symbolic rule, the symbolic rule can be injected as a neural rule, and participate in further consolidation / generalization / learning.  Could this be a significant advantage?

The situation isn't too complicated.  We only have two main objectives: forward inference and learning / mem consolidation.  We have two competing sub-systems: neural and symbolic, but they are compatible with each other by having the same logical structure.  But it is the subtle interplay between the two sub-systems that will give our model distinct advantages. Is this viewpoint clear? If yes then let's make a plan to implement the system step by step with small tests to validate each step.

Nice.  We have worked out a sort of abstract rewriting scheme where the "predicate" position is allowed to have variables.  This may be akin to second order logc.  And I think that added expressiveness is suitable for AGI, although we seem to have lost the rigor of having a well-defined and typed logic.  Should we go ahead with that or you have a better suggestion?  If not, let's go ahead.

I'd like the logic to be very expressive or "universal" in some sense.  For example, Russell's paradox can be avoided by having a fuzzy truth value at 0.5 which is neither true or false.  Then our AGI can think about such problems without going astray as in "EFSQ".  Do you think our current logic with Davidsonian parsing still retains that ability to reason about arbitrary paradoxes?

We have not talked about fuzzy truth values.  I have formulated a theory of fuzzy-probabilistic logic (with probabilities distributed over fuzzy values) which I think is mathematically rigorous and suitable for AGI.  It may be easier to implement on the symbolic engine, but seems more difficult to implement in DLN.  What do you think?

1) I want to keep the DLN part simple as otherwise it would be hard to train.
2) can you explain a bit about paraconsist logic?  is it needed in addition to fuzziness?

Another trick, which I have not fully fleshed out, has to do with the symbolic engine and NL rule injection.  But I have not figured how exactly can the symbolic engine accelerate DLN training.

Thanks for the suggestions, I am slowly digesting them.  First, in the GA method, are we solely relying on AR signals for the loss function?  If GA shows early convergence, why not use GA all the way?  Is GA likely to show early convergence, on large, real-life NL corpora?  What else can we exploit other than AR signals, perhaps annotated data?

1) So GA is good for exploring the global landscape quickly, is that the correct impression?
2) Perhaps we can organize the rule-store from concrete to abstract (specific to general), is this advantageous? can this help rules to converge faster? 
3) As the system reads in NL data, it may encounter some sentences that are already in "rule form", eg. "water always flows downhill" or "counterfactuals are in past tense".  It seems that these can be directly integrated into either the DLN side or the symbolic side.  I think this constitutes the greatest accelerating factor, or I may be mistaken?

If we add many rules to the DLN side it may slow down learning significantly (but then again maybe not, as we're not updating all rules per iteration).  Another question is whether we can let DLN and symbolic engine operate side by side with cross-interactions, without any adverse effects?  It seems okay.  Finally, there should be a process of "grokking" or "comprehension" in which new knowledge is absorbed into memory while maintaining logical coherence.  This may be a necessary step, and humans do that too, which explains why humans learn slowly.

Yes, this is very good progress and gives conceptual clarity to the whole project.  Can you summarize in an .md somewhere?  Then we proceed full-speed towards the end goal of training with large, real-life data.
